items.title: Equilibria, Lyapunov stability and asymptotic stability of an autonomous first-order system
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 6.5 (Stability of fixed points), printed pages 198-200, licensed author preliminary version
D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 6 (Non-inertial frames)

items.title: Invariant sets, orbital stability of an invariant set, and linear stability of an equilibrium
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map; retain the convention of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] that a solution means a solution of $z'(t)=F(z(t))$, read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], and that it is defined for all $t\ge0$ when its interval contains $[0,\infty)$. A maximal solution means one with no proper extension, as defined there; the invariance and stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions through time $0$, not their arbitrary local restrictions. No existence or uniqueness is asserted for an arbitrary $F$.

**Invariant sets.** A set $S\subseteq U$ is **forward invariant** (for this system) when every maximal solution $z$ with $z(0)\in S$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $z(t)\in S$ for all $t\ge0$.

**Distance to a set.** For a nonempty $S\subseteq U$ define

$$\operatorname{dist}(z,S):=\inf\{\,\|z-s\|_2:s\in S\,\}\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^n),$$

the infimum of a nonempty set of nonnegative reals that is bounded below, computed for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the Euclidean closure of $S$ by

$$\overline S:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\text{for every }\varepsilon>0\text{ there is }s\in S\text{ with }\|z-s\|_2<\varepsilon\}.$$

The map $z\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(z,S)$ is nonnegative and vanishes exactly on $\overline S$: by the defining property of the infimum, $\operatorname{dist}(z,S)=0$ exactly when every positive-radius Euclidean ball about $z$ meets $S$. When $S=\{z_*\}$ is a singleton, $\operatorname{dist}(z,S)=\|z-z_*\|_2$.

**Orbital stability.** Let $S\subseteq U$ be nonempty and forward invariant. Then $S$ is **orbitally stable** when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\operatorname{dist}(z(0),S)<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\operatorname{dist}(z(t),S)<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

It is **asymptotically orbitally stable** when it is orbitally stable and there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution with $\operatorname{dist}(z(0),S)<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(z(t),S)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

**Linear stability.** Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium of $F$ and suppose $F$ is totally differentiable at $z_*$ in the sense of [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with total derivative $DF(z_*):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$; write $L:=DF(z_*)$. The **linearized system** at $z_*$ is the autonomous linear system

$$y'(t)=L\,y(t).$$

The equilibrium $z_*$ is **linearly stable** when every maximal solution $y$ of the linearized system ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and is bounded on $[0,\infty)$, that is, there is a real constant $C\ge0$ with $\|y(t)\|_2\le C$ for every $t\ge0$. It is **linearly asymptotically stable** when every maximal solution of the linearized system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|y(t)\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Sections 3.2 and 6.5, printed pages 61-67 and 198-200
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 2.2 (small oscillations and equilibrium)

items.title: Hyperbolic equilibria, hyperbolic fixed points, periodic orbits, limit cycles and homoclinic trajectories
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map; a solution means a solution of $z'(t)=F(z(t))$ as in [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]].

For a real linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$, define its **complex-linear extension** $A_{\mathbb C}:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ by $A_{\mathbb C}(x+iy):=Ax+iAy$ for $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$. In both spectral definitions below, an eigenvalue means an eigenvalue of $A_{\mathbb C}$ over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]] with field $F=\mathbb C$); $\operatorname{Re}\lambda$ and $|\lambda|$ are the real part and modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]].

**Hyperbolic equilibrium.** Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium of $F$ and suppose $F$ is totally differentiable at $z_*$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) with total derivative $DF(z_*)$. Then $z_*$ is **hyperbolic** when no eigenvalue of the real matrix of $DF(z_*)$ has real part $0$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**Hyperbolic fixed point of a map.** Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\varphi:V\to V$ be a map and let $p\in V$ satisfy $\varphi(p)=p$. Suppose $\varphi$ is totally differentiable at $p$. Then $p$ is a **hyperbolic fixed point** of $\varphi$ when no eigenvalue of $D\varphi(p)$ has modulus $1$.

**Periodic solutions and periodic orbits.** A solution $z:\mathbb R\to U$ is **$T$-periodic** for $T>0$ when $z(t+T)=z(t)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$, and **periodic** when it is $T$-periodic for some $T>0$. It is **nonconstant** when $z(t_1)\ne z(t_2)$ for some $t_1,t_2$. The **image** of a periodic solution is $\{z(t):t\in\mathbb R\}$; a subset of $U$ is a **periodic orbit** when it is the image of a nonconstant periodic solution. A number $T>0$ is a **least period** of $z$ when $T$ is a period of $z$ and no $T'\in(0,T)$ is a period of $z$.

**Limit cycle.** A periodic orbit $S\subseteq U$ is a **limit cycle** when it is **isolated**: there is an open set $W\subseteq U$ with $S\subseteq W$ such that the image of every nonconstant periodic solution lying in $W$ equals $S$; equivalently, no other periodic orbit of the system is contained in $W$. Stability or attraction of $S$ is a separate property and is not part of the definition.

**Homoclinic and heteroclinic trajectories.** A solution $z$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$ is **homoclinic** to the equilibrium $z_*$ when $z(t)\to z_*$ as $t\to+\infty$ and as $t\to-\infty$ and $z$ is not the constant solution $z\equiv z_*$. It is **heteroclinic** from $z_*$ to $z_{**}$ when $z_*\ne z_{**}$ are equilibria and $z(t)\to z_{**}$ as $t\to+\infty$ and $z(t)\to z_*$ as $t\to-\infty$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 9.1 (hyperbolic systems), printed pages 253-255, and Section 6.4 (the Poincare map), printed page 198
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 2.2 and Chapter 4

items.title: The stroboscopic (time-$P$) map of a $P$-periodic first-order system
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $P>0$, and let $F:\mathbb R\times U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map that is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, in the sense of the hypotheses of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]], and that is **$P$-periodic**:

$$F(t+P,z)=F(t,z)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R,\ z\in U).$$

Consider the first-order system $x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$ of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $\mathbb R\times U$. For $z\in U$ let

$$x_z:J_z\longrightarrow U$$

be the unique maximal solution of the initial value problem $x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$, $x(0)=z$; here $J_z$ is the open maximal interval of existence containing $0$, and by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] every solution of this initial value problem is a restriction of $x_z$ ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[def-interval]]).

The **domain of the stroboscopic map** is

$$D_P:=\{\,z\in U:[0,P]\subseteq J_z\,\},$$

the set of initial states whose solution exists over one full period. The **stroboscopic map** (or **time-$P$ map**) of the system is the function

$$\theta_P:D_P\longrightarrow U,\qquad \theta_P(z):=x_z(P).$$

This is a well-defined function: for $z\in D_P$ the interval $J_z$ contains $P$, so $x_z(P)$ is a point of $U$, and by the uniqueness clause of the maximal-solution theorem the value $x_z(P)$ does not depend on any choice, since $x_z$ is the only maximal solution through $(0,z)$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 6.4 (the Poincare map, Problem 6.14) and Sections 4.6-4.7 on periodic equations, printed pages 198 and 133-141
D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 6 (motion in a rotating frame, periodic forcing examples)

items.title: Iterates of the stroboscopic map, and equilibria as fixed points
items.statement:
Retain all notation and hypotheses of [[def-cm-stroboscopic-map]]: $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open, $P>0$, and $F:\mathbb R\times U\to\mathbb R^n$ is continuous, locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and $P$-periodic.

1. If $z\in D_P$ and $\theta_P(z)\in D_P$, then $[0,2P]\subseteq J_z$ and

$$\theta_P(\theta_P(z))=x_z(2P).$$

2. If $z_*\in U$ satisfies $F(t,z_*)=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$, then $z_*\in D_P$ and $\theta_P(z_*)=z_*$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 6.4 and Section 4.6, printed pages 198 and 133-141

items.title: Constrained configurations, the mass matrix and the mass metric
items.statement:
Let $N\ge1$; the ambient dimension is $3N$. Identify $\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the $N$-fold product $(\mathbb R^3)^N$ and write a point as $x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^3$, explicitly $x_i(k):=x(3(i-1)+k)$ for $1\le i\le N$ and $0\le k<3$; the Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_2,$$

with $\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle_2$ the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $d\ge0$ and let $Q$ be a smooth $d$-dimensional manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) and let

$$X:Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$$

be a smooth map. The manifold $Q$ is the **configuration space** and $X$ is the **configuration map**; the pair $(Q,X)$ is called a **particle configuration** when $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ and $X$ is the inclusion ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]), and a **parametrized configuration** otherwise. For $q\in Q$ the intrinsic differential is $dX_q:T_qQ\to T_{X(q)}\mathbb R^{3N}$ as in [[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]] ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]] for the tangent space). For $a\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ and the coordinate function $\pi_k(x):=x(k)$, define $\iota_a:T_a\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by $\iota_a(w)(k):=w([\pi_k])$ for $0\le k<3N$. This is the standard linear isomorphism: in the identity chart the coordinate derivations form a basis by [[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]], and evaluation on coordinate germs sends that basis to the standard unit vectors. Throughout this item and its mass-metric formulas, the notation $dX_q(u)$ in Euclidean expressions abbreviates $\iota_{X(q)}(dX_q(u))$. In particular its components are $u([\pi_k\circ X])$, so this convention retains the usual Jacobian and inclusion formulas.

Let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ be **masses**. The **mass matrix** is the linear map $M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ acting on each block by $M(x_1,\dots,x_N)=(m_1x_1,\dots,m_Nx_N)$; its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_iI_3$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

The **mass metric** of $(Q,X,m_1,\dots,m_N)$ is the family of maps

$$G_q:T_qQ\times T_qQ\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad G_q(u,v):=\langle dX_q(u),\,M\,dX_q(v)\rangle_{3N},$$

for $q\in Q$ and $u,v\in T_qQ$. The **kinetic energy** of a tangent vector $v\in T_qQ$ is

$$T_q(v):=\tfrac12\,G_q(v,v).$$

Each $G_q$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the real vector space $T_qQ$ in the sense of [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]; that the family depends smoothly on $q$ means that in every smooth local chart of $Q$ the coefficient functions $q\mapsto G_q(\partial_i,\partial_j)$ are smooth, and is stated in the smoothness remark below.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 2.1 (constraints, generalized coordinates) and Section 3.1 (configuration space)
R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Chapter 3

items.title: The mass metric is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and positive definite exactly when the configuration differential is injective
items.statement:
Let $N\ge1$, let $Q$ be a smooth manifold, let $X:Q\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ be smooth, let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $G_q$ be the mass metric of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].

1. For every $q\in Q$ the map $G_q$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $T_qQ$.
2. $G_q(u,u)=\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\|dX_q(u)_i\|_2^2\ge 0$ for every $u\in T_qQ$, so $G_q$ is positive semidefinite.
3. $G_q$ is positive definite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]) if and only if $dX_q$ is injective. In particular, if $X$ is an immersion ([[def-immersion-submersion-and-constant-rank-map]]) then $G_q$ is positive definite for every $q$.
4. If $b_1,\dots,b_n$ is an ordered basis of $T_qQ$ and $A$ is the matrix whose $j$-th column is the coordinate vector of $dX_q(b_j)$ in the standard basis of $\mathbb R^{3N}$, then the matrix of the bilinear form $G_q$ in this basis is $A^{\mathsf T}MA$, with $M$ the mass matrix.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 2.1 and Section 3.1
R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 3.9 (inertia of rigid motions)

items.title: Material regions, densities and their mass
items.statement:
A **material region** is a nonempty, bounded, open subset $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. This region predicate is choice-free and does not assume a density or measure.

For the following **Lebesgue density and mass construction**, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]): [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] supplies the measure $\lambda_3$ on its Lebesgue sigma-algebra ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure]]). Since $B$ is open, it is Lebesgue measurable by the Borel-measurability theorem ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Put $\mathcal L_B:=\{E\cap B:E\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)\}$ and $\lambda_B(C):=\lambda_3(C)$ for $C\in\mathcal L_B$. The trace family $\mathcal L_B$ is a sigma-algebra on $B$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]); countable additivity of $\lambda_B$ follows by applying that of $\lambda_3$ to disjoint trace-measurable sets, so $(B,\mathcal L_B,\lambda_B)$ is a measure space ([[def-measure]]). In the displays below, $\int_B\rho\,d\lambda_3$ means the Lebesgue integral of $\rho$ on this measure space ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). A **density** on $B$ is a measurable function

$$\rho:B\longrightarrow[0,\infty)$$

measurable as a map from $(B,\mathcal L_B)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ ([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and integrable on $(B,\mathcal L_B,\lambda_B)$; the **mass** of the pair $(B,\rho)$ is

$$\operatorname{mass}(B,\rho):=\int_B\rho\,d\lambda_3\ \in[0,\infty).$$

For this scalar function, **bounded** means that some $M<\infty$ satisfies $0\le\rho(X)\le M$ for every $X\in B$. **Continuous** means that for every $X\in B$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $Y\in B$ and $\|X-Y\|_2<\delta$ imply $|\rho(X)-\rho(Y)|<\varepsilon$. For $k\ge1$, **of class $C^k$ on $B$** means that every iterated coordinate partial derivative of order at most $k$ exists on $B$ and is continuous there; no extension to $\partial B$ is required unless a consuming statement says so. A **measured material region** is a triple $(B,\rho,m)$ with $m=\operatorname{mass}(B,\rho)$ recorded.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 1.8 (extensive properties and their densities) and Section 4.2 (conservation of mass), printed pages 12-14 and 104
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 5 (the motion of deformable bodies)

items.title: Traction fields and stress matrices representing them
items.statement:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a spatial set and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a time interval. No openness of $\Omega$ or regularity of a traction map is assumed by this definition; consumers impose any needed additional hypotheses. Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

A **traction field** is a map

$$t:S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$

read with the following convention: $t(n)$ is the force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$ points upon the material on the other side**, at the point of a surface whose unit normal is $n$. The dependence of $t$ on position and time is suppressed in this notation; a traction **field on a set** $\Omega\times I$ is a map $t:\Omega\times I\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, and all statements below apply to each fixed $(y,s)$.

For $v\in\mathbb R^3$ use one-based component labels $v_i:=v(i-1)$, and for $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ use $\sigma_{ij}:=\sigma(i-1,j-1)$, where $1\le i,j\le3$; $e_i$ is the vector with value $1$ at $i-1$ and $0$ at the other two indices. Define the matrix-vector action $\sigma v\in\mathbb R^3$ by $(\sigma v)(k):=\sum_{j<3}\sigma(k,j)v(j)$ for $0\le k<3$, equivalently $(\sigma v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\sigma_{ij}v_j$. It is the rectangular product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] after identifying $v$ with the column matrix $C_v(j,0):=v(j)$ and the result with its sole column.

A matrix $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) **represents** the traction field $t$ when

$$t(n)=\sigma n\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2,$$

the product being the matrix-vector action defined above. A matrix representing a traction field is called a **stress matrix** for it.

The **reversed normal convention** is the identity $t(-n)=-t(n)$; it is a property some traction fields have and is not part of the definition. A traction field is **normal** when $t(n)$ is a real multiple of $n$ for every $n$, and **purely tangential** when $\langle t(n),n\rangle_2=0$ for every $n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.3 (force, Cauchy's hypothesis, Remarks (b)-(e)), printed pages 105-110
MIT OpenCourseWare 12.005, Applications of Continuum Mechanics, Lecture 3: tensors, stress, Cauchy tetrahedron and Cauchy's formula

items.title: Affine time space with Euclidean simultaneous slices and adapted charts
items.statement:
Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $4$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $\tau:V\to\mathbb R$ be a surjective linear map ([[def-linear-map]]). Put

$$K:=\ker\tau=\{v\in V:\tau(v)=0\},$$

the kernel of $\tau$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]). The kernel is a linear subspace ([[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]), so the quotient vector space $V/K$ is defined ([[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]]). The first isomorphism theorem gives the linear isomorphism $V/K\to\operatorname{im}\tau=\mathbb R$, $v+K\mapsto\tau(v)$ ([[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-for-vector-spaces]]). Since $\mathbb R$ has the one-element standard basis, $\dim\mathbb R=1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] with $F=\mathbb R$ and $n=1$); rank-nullity for the surjective map $\tau$ therefore gives $\dim K=4-1=3$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

Let $g$ be an inner product on $K$ in the sense of [[def-inner-product-space]]: a symmetric positive definite $\mathbb R$-bilinear form $g:K\times K\to\mathbb R$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set equipped with an action of the additive group of $V$, written $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$, that is free and transitive: explicitly, $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$; write $q-p$ for that unique vector. The identities $p+(q-p)=q$, $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ and $q-p=-(p-q)$ follow from the axioms together with uniqueness of the displacement. Such a set is an **affine space modelled on $V$**, and its elements are **events**. (This formulation restates the affine-space structure used here so that the item is self-contained; the general theory of affine spaces is supplied by the special-relativity collection for its own consumers.)

Fix an orientation of $K$ in the sense of [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]; this is a chosen orientation class, not a chosen spatial basis.

An **adapted chart** for the data $(V,\tau,g,A)$ is a triple $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ consisting of

1. an origin $o\in A$;
2. a vector $u\in V$ with $\tau(u)=1$;
3. an ordered basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $K$ that is $g$-orthonormal and positively oriented with respect to the fixed orientation of $K$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

An adapted chart exists for every such set of data and fixed orientation, by clause 3 of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

For spatial coordinate vectors $x\in\mathbb R^3$, this item uses the one-based labels $x_i:=x(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le3$; thus $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ lists the values at $0,1,2$ of the function-space vector of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The labels $e_1,e_2,e_3$ name the corresponding ordered spatial basis; they do not change the underlying index set of $\mathbb R^3$.

The **adapted coordinates** of a point $p\in A$ in this chart are the pair $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ determined by

$$p=o+tu+\sum_{i=1}^{3}x_ie_i,$$

when such a pair exists (existence and uniqueness are [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]], so that the notation is defined for every $p$). The number $t$ is the **time coordinate** and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ the **spatial coordinate vector** of $p$ in the chart. When $K$ is identified with $\mathbb R^3$ through the coordinates in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the assignment $p\mapsto(t,x)$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$.

**Simultaneous slices.** For $t\in\mathbb R$ set

$$A_t:=\{p\in A:\tau(p-o)=t\}.$$

The family $\{A_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R}$ is the family of **simultaneous slices** of the chart. Each $A_t$ is an affine space modelled on $K$; the derivation is immediate from the affine identities and linearity of $\tau$ and is recorded in [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]. The **slice distance** of two points $p,q$ in a common slice $A_t$ is

$$d_g(p,q):=\sqrt{g(p-q,\,p-q)},$$

the square root taken in $\mathbb R$; this is defined because $p-q\in K$ for points of a common slice. In adapted coordinates $d_g(p,q)=\|x(p)-x(q)\|_2$, with $\|\cdot\|_2$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

references.title: D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 1.2.1 (Galilean relativity: translations, rotations, boosts, absolute time), printed pages 5-7
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1 (rigid body kinematics, orthogonal matrices)

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of adapted coordinates, and the affine structure of simultaneous slices
items.statement:
Let $(V,\tau,g,A)$ and an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ be as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]].

1. Every $p\in A$ has exactly one pair $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ with

$$p=o+tu+\sum_{i=1}^3x_ie_i,$$

so the adapted-coordinate map $\iota:A\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ of that definition is well defined, and it is a bijection.

2. For every $t\in\mathbb R$ the simultaneous slice $A_t=\{p:\tau(p-o)=t\}$ is an affine space modelled on $K=\ker\tau$, and for $p,q\in A_t$ one has $p-q\in K$ with $p-q=\sum_i(x_i(p)-x_i(q))e_i$ and

$$d_g(p,q)=\|x(p)-x(q)\|_2.$$

3. For every set of data $(V,\tau,g,A)$ and fixed orientation of $K$ satisfying [[def-cm-affine-time-space]], at least one adapted chart exists. No origin, time vector or spatial basis is distinguished by this existence assertion.

references.title: D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 1.2.1, printed pages 5-7

items.title: Transformation between adapted charts and its kinematic consequences
items.statement:
Let $(V,\tau,g,A)$ be as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] and let $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ and $(o',u',(e_1',e_2',e_3'))$ be two adapted charts, with coordinate functions $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,v\in\mathbb R^3$ and a matrix $R\in O(3)$ such that for every $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a.$$

If $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1',e_2',e_3')$ are both positively oriented for the fixed orientation of $K$, then $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]).

2. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a map whose first-chart time coordinate satisfies $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all $s\in I$. Write $x(s):=x(\gamma(s))$ and $y(s):=x'(\gamma(s))$. The regularity hypothesis below means that this coordinate function $x:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuously differentiable (respectively, twice continuously differentiable); no additional smooth structure on $A$ is assumed. If $x$ is continuously differentiable then $y$ is continuously differentiable with

$$y'(s)=R\,x'(s)+v\qquad(s\in I),$$

and if $x$ is twice continuously differentiable then $y''(s)=R\,x''(s)$ for all $s\in I$. Equivalently, in the differentiated variables of the two charts, $dx'/dt'=R\,dx/dt+v$ and $d^2x'/dt'^2=R\,d^2x/dt^2$.

3. Consequently $x''=0$ on $I$ if and only if $y''=0$ on $I$: the two charts agree on which time-parametrized curves have zero coordinate acceleration.

references.title: D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 1.2.1 (translations, rotations, boosts and absolute time), printed pages 5-7
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48

items.title: Angular velocity of a moving frame and the rotating-frame acceleration identity
items.statement:
Use one-based labels $z_i:=z(i-1)$ and $A_{ij}:=A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i,j\le3$, so the displayed components correspond in order to the imported coordinates $0,1,2$. Matrix-vector products mean $(Az)(k):=\sum_{j<3}A(k,j)z(j)$, obtained from the rectangular product by representing $z$ as the column $C_z(j,0)=z(j)$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval, let $R:I\to SO(3)$ and $c:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice continuously differentiable in the sense that all entries of $R$ and all components of $c$ have continuous second derivatives, and put

$$\Omega(t):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)\qquad(t\in I).$$

1. $\Omega(t)$ is skew-symmetric for every $t\in I$, that is $\Omega(t)^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega(t)$.
2. For every $t\in I$ there is exactly one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ such that

$$\Omega(t)z=\omega(t)\times z\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^3),$$

the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Its components in the standard basis are $\omega(t)=(-\Omega_{23}(t),\Omega_{13}(t),-\Omega_{12}(t))$. Since $R$ is $C^2$, $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'$ and hence $\omega$ are $C^1$; thus $\omega'(t)$ in clause 3 is defined.
3. If $y:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is twice continuously differentiable and

$$x(t):=R(t)y(t)+c(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

then for every $t\in I$

$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}x''(t)=y''(t)+2\,\omega(t)\times y'(t)+\omega'(t)\times y(t)+\omega(t)\times\bigl(\omega(t)\times y(t)\bigr)+R(t)^{\mathsf T}c''(t).$$

4. For every $t\in I$ and $z\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|R(t)z\|_2=\|z\|_2$: the rotation part of the change of coordinates preserves Euclidean norms ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1.1 (angular velocity and the antisymmetry of omega), printed pages 47-49
D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 6 (non-inertial frames: centrifugal and Coriolis terms), printed pages 101-110

items.title: The orthogonal group $O(3)$ and the rotation group $SO(3)$
items.statement:
Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

references.title: J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2003), Example 8.33 (the orthogonal group) and Example 8.35 (the special orthogonal group), printed pages 194-196
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48

items.title: $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group, with $R^{-1}=R^{\mathsf T}$
items.statement:
In the notation of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]:

1. $I_3\in SO(3)$, and for all $R,S\in SO(3)$ the matrices $RS$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$ again lie in $SO(3)$; moreover $\det R=1$, $R$ is invertible, and its inverse is $R^{\mathsf T}$, so also $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$.
2. Consequently $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]).

references.title: J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2003), Example 8.35, printed page 196
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48

items.title: $SO(3)$ is a compact three-dimensional embedded submanifold of $M_3(\mathbb R)$, with tangent space the matrices $R\Omega$ for skew $\Omega$
items.statement:
Identify $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ as in [[def-matrix-space]], with the Euclidean metric of that identification ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

1. $SO(3)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ of dimension $3$, and it is both open and closed in the subset topology of $O(3)$ inside $M_3(\mathbb R)$.
2. For every $R\in SO(3)$ the tangent space is

$$T_RSO(3)=\{\,R\Omega:\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R),\ \Omega^{\mathsf T}=-\Omega\,\}.$$

3. $SO(3)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

references.title: J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2003), Examples 8.33 and 8.35, printed pages 195-196
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48

items.title: A labeling containing two independent vectors has trivial $SO(3)$-stabilizer
items.statement:
For $S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, its **pointwise $SO(3)$ stabilizer** is

$$\operatorname{Stab}_{SO(3)}(S):=\{R\in SO(3):Rs=s\text{ for every }s\in S\}.$$

Let $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$ be linearly independent and let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty set with $u,v\in S$. If $R\in SO(3)$ satisfies $Rs=s$ for every $s\in S$, then $R=I_3$.

Equivalently, $\operatorname{Stab}_{SO(3)}(S)=\{I_3\}$. The conclusion uses only the two indicated independent vectors; no assumption that $0\in S$ is made.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48
J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2003), Example 8.35, printed page 196

items.title: Worked change of adapted chart with a rotation, a boost and a spatial shift
items.statement:
Take $V=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $(t,x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $\tau(t,x_1,x_2,x_3)=t$, so that $K=\{0\}\times\mathbb R^3$ with the standard inner product $g$, and take $A=V$ as an affine space over itself. Let the first adapted chart be the standard one, $o=0$, $u=e_0$, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the standard basis of $K$. Let the second adapted chart be

$$o'=e_2,\qquad u'=e_0+e_1,\qquad e_1'=e_2,\quad e_2'=-e_1,\quad e_3'=e_3,$$

which is adapted: $\tau(u')=1$, and $(e_1',e_2',e_3')$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal basis of $K$.

For a point with first coordinates $(t,x_1,x_2,x_3)$, equating the two expansions gives $t'=t$, $x_2=x_1'+1$ and $x_1=t'-x_2'$, that is

$$x'_1=x_2-1,\qquad x'_2=t-x_1,\qquad x'_3=x_3,$$

which is the transformation $x'=Rx+vt+a$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]] with $b=0$,

$$R=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad a=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}.$$

The matrix $R$ satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$, so $R\in SO(3)$.

references.title: D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 1.2.1, printed pages 5-7

items.title: The rotating-frame acceleration identity for a uniform rotation about an axis
items.statement:
Let $\nu>0$ and define $R:\mathbb R\to SO(3)$ by the rotation about the third standard axis through angle $\nu t$:

$$R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\nu t&-\sin\nu t&0\\ \sin\nu t&\cos\nu t&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Then $R(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t$, and $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'$ is

$$\Omega(t)=\nu\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

The angular-velocity vector of [[lem-cm-moving-frame-acceleration-identity]] is $\boldsymbol\omega(t)=(0,0,\nu)$, independent of $t$. For any twice continuously differentiable $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, put $x(t):=R(t)y(t)$ and let $c:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be identically zero. That lemma gives

$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}x''(t)=y''(t)+2\,\boldsymbol\omega\times y'(t)+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times y(t))\qquad(x=Ry).$$

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1.1, printed pages 47-49
D. Tong, Dynamics and Relativity (Cambridge lecture notes, 2013), Section 6, printed pages 101-110

items.title: The mass metric of a particle constrained to the unit sphere in spherical coordinates
items.statement:
Let $Q:=S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\|x\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]), with the smooth two-dimensional embedded structure supplied by [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] applied to $F(x)=\langle x,x\rangle_2$ at the regular value $1$ (verified below), let $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3$ be the inclusion, and let $m>0$ be the mass of one particle, so that the mass matrix of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]] is $M=mI_3$.

The mass metric of the inclusion is $G_q(u,v)=m\langle u,v\rangle_2$ for $u,v\in T_qS^2$, hence positive definite at every point by [[lem-cm-mass-metric-positivity]]. On $D:=(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ consider the parametrization

$$\Psi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta).$$

Its image is the open subset $U:=S^2\setminus\{x\in S^2:x_2=0,\ x_1\ge0\}$, which excludes the poles and the longitude seam. The map $\Psi:D\to U$ is a diffeomorphism; in the manifold-to-coordinate convention the chart is $(U,\Psi^{-1})$. Its differential is injective on $D$, and in the coordinate basis $(\partial_\theta,\partial_\varphi)$ the mass metric has the classical spherical form

$$G\bigl(\dot\theta\partial_\theta+\dot\varphi\partial_\varphi,\ \dot\theta\partial_\theta+\dot\varphi\partial_\varphi\bigr)=m\bigl(\dot\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2\bigr).$$

Equivalently, the kinetic energy of a tangent vector with coordinate velocity $(\dot\theta,\dot\varphi)$ is $T=\tfrac m2(\dot\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1 (configuration space) and Section 2.1 (generalized coordinates)
R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Appendix C (curvilinear coordinates), printed pages 160-162

items.title: A collinear labeling admits a nontrivial rotation
items.statement: Every nonempty labeling $S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ determines the rotation: if $R\in SO(3)$ satisfies $Rs=s$ for every $s\in S$, then $R=I_3$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 3.1, printed pages 46-48

items.title: A closed field on a star-shaped domain with its radial primitive computed
items.statement:
On $U=\mathbb R^2$, which is star-shaped about the origin ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), consider the $C^1$ field $F(x,y):=(2xy,\,x^2)$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]). Its potential

$$\phi(x,y):=x^2y$$

has gradient $\nabla\phi=(2xy,x^2)=F$, so $F$ is exact with potential $\phi$. The closed field condition $\partial_1F_0=\partial_0F_1$ holds as well, and the radial formula of the published Poincare lemma returns exactly $\phi$:

$$\int_0^1\bigl\langle F(t(x,y)),(x,y)\bigr\rangle_2\,dt=\int_0^1 3x^2y\,t^2\,dt=x^2y.$$

references.title: J.-B. Campesato, Poincare Lemma, section 2 (the radial primitive)
J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2003), Theorem 17.14 (the Poincare lemma), printed page 447

items.title: The stroboscopic map of the plane oscillator
items.statement:
Let $\omega>0$ and let $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$, $F(t,z_1,z_2):=(z_2,-\omega^2z_1)$, the vector field of the undamped plane oscillator. Since $F$ does not depend on $t$, it is $P$-periodic for every $P>0$; it is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, so [[def-cm-stroboscopic-map]] applies for every $P>0$.

For $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb R^2$ the curve

$$x_z(t)=\Bigl(z_1\cos\omega t+\frac{z_2}{\omega}\sin\omega t,\ -\omega z_1\sin\omega t+z_2\cos\omega t\Bigr)$$

is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and solves $x'=F(t,x)$ with $x(0)=z$. Hence $D_P=\mathbb R^2$ for every $P>0$, and the stroboscopic map is

$$\theta_P(z)=\Bigl(z_1\cos\omega P+\frac{z_2}{\omega}\sin\omega P,\ -\omega z_1\sin\omega P+z_2\cos\omega P\Bigr).$$

In particular, for $P=2\pi/\omega$ the map $\theta_P$ is the identity of $\mathbb R^2$, so every initial state is a fixed point; for $P=\pi/\omega$ it is $\theta_P(z)=-z$, whose only fixed point is $0$.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 3.2 (linear systems) and Section 6.4 (the Poincare map), printed pages 61-67 and 198
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), Section 2.2 and Section 4.1 (linear oscillators and Hamilton's equations)
